newsitem.title: USA: NFL-TOP CHEESHEAD IN TOWN FOR SUPER BOWL.
newsitem.headline: NFL-TOP CHEESHEAD IN TOWN FOR SUPER BOWL.

text.p: The Big Easy became the big cheesy this week as Green Bay fans descended on New Orleans, and the top cheesehead was in town to celebrate the Packers' return to the Super Bowl after 29 years.
The Governor of Wisconsin, Tommy Thompson, was seen in at least one Bourbon Street watering hole among the Super Bowl revellers on Friday night.

Thompson, flanked by Louisiana state police, walked into the Old Opera House bar and was immediately recognised and warmly greeted by fellow Packer backers decked in cheesehead hats, cheese ties and other assorted green and gold attire.
"The whole state, everybody, cares what happens to our football team," Green Bay coach Mike Holmgren beamed earlier this week as he prepared for Super Bowl XXXI against the New England Patriots.
Sure, New England fans are enthusiastic, but they would be just as happy to see the Red Sox in baseball's World Series or the Celtics back in the National Basketball Association Finals.

In Green Bay, the smallest major league city in North America, the Packers are the only game in town -- a town in which babies are born into green and gold receiving blankets and immediately put on waiting lists for Packers season tickets.

Unlike any other professional sports team, the Packers are owned by members of the community -- who bought shares for $25 each in 1952 in order to keep the financially strapped club forever in Green Bay.
Only in recent years was the practice of leaving Packers season tickets to offspring in wills banned. The waiting list for tickets is now about 40 years.
"Until you get there and live there and experience it, it's hard to describe," Holmgren said. "We have the best fans in the world."
When the Packers played the San Francisco 49ers in miserable, driving sleet and freezing rain in the playoffs three weeks ago, there were exactly three no-shows in the stands at Lambeau field.

The following week when the Packers beat the Carolina Panthers in the NFC championship game, Holmgren remembers marvelling at the sight of all the fans remaining in the stadium to celebrate long after the game had ended despite sub-freezing temperatures.
The love affair between the Packers and their fans is unique and unconditional.

There is no more spontaneous demonstration of mutual adoration and trust between professional athletes and fans than when one of the Packers leaps into the stands, into the arms of fans at Lambeau Field, after scoring a touchdown.
Green Bay defensive end Sean Jones said when one of his teammates jumps into the seats behind the end zone, "you can feel the love even if you're not the one in the stands."
And Holmgren points out that the fanatic adulation is not limited to Lambeau field.
"Every time we go on the road there is a good group of people in green jerseys with those crazy cheesehead hats on, and that's nice to see. It really helps the football team."
Have no fear, coach, the cheeseheads have arrived in force in New Orleans.
